title: Why you have to leave
translation: You hear people say: "If your heart is in it, it doesn't matter where you live. You can stay at home, mix with people, and still work toward the next life. What's so hard about that?" They don't understand the next life at all.

If you really feel how short this life is, and you're determined to get free of the round of birth and death, how could you enjoy serving a lord from morning to night and running a household? The mind is pulled along by whatever is around it. Without quiet, you can't follow the path.

We're not as strong as the people of old. Even in the mountains, you can't live without some way to keep off hunger and the weather. So now and then, when the chance comes, you may do something that looks like clinging to the world. Of course you may. But to say "Then what was the point of leaving? If that's how it is, why did you bother?" is just wrong.

Once someone has taken the step and become a monk, he still has to get by in the world, and he may want things. But he'll never want them like the greedy people with power. A paper blanket, hemp clothes, one bowl of food, soup made from weeds: how much does that cost anyone? What he needs is easy to get, and he's soon satisfied. And because he's ashamed to do wrong in a monk's robes, he mostly keeps away from the bad and closer to the good.
If being born human counts for anything, find some way to get out of the world. If all you do is grab, and you never head for awakening, how are you any different from an animal?

literal: Those who say, 'If one has the will for the Way, it will not depend on where one lives; even if one stays at home and mixes with people, how could it be hard to pray for the next life?' are people who know nothing at all of the next life.

Truly, if one finds this world fleeting and thinks one will surely get out of birth and death, what pleasure would there be, how could one be keen on the business of serving a lord morning and evening and looking after a household?
The mind is a thing that is drawn by circumstances and shifts, so unless it is quiet, the Way is hard to practise.

One's capacity does not reach that of the people of old, and even if one goes into the mountains and forests, without means to relieve hunger and keep off storms one cannot live, so naturally, when an occasion arises, why would there not be things that look like greed for the world?
But to say for that reason, 'There is no point in having turned away. If it is like that, why did you abandon (the world)?' is utterly wrong.
After all, a person who has once entered the Way and (still) attends to the world, even if he has wishes, cannot be like the great greed of people with power.
A paper blanket, hemp clothes, the provision of one bowl, soup of goosefoot: how much expense would they cause anyone?
What he seeks is easy, and his heart will surely soon be satisfied.
Since there is also shame before his (monk's) appearance, though that is so, he is mostly distant from evil and draws near to good.
As a sign of having been born human, one would wish somehow to escape the world.
Those who work only at greed and do not head toward enlightenment: would they not be no different from all the beasts?

notes.text: {道心|だうしん}: the will to follow the Buddhist path. {後世|ごせ}: the next life, and the hope of being reborn in paradise instead of being born again in this world.
かは: a rhetorical question, 'how could it be hard? (It isn't.)'. This is the opponent's argument. Kenkō answers: 更に … ぬ, 'not at all'.
{生死|しやうじ}: the endless cycle of birth and death. To get out of it is the goal of Buddhist practice.
{勇|いさ}まし here means 'keen, eager' (the 1925 edition: 'in the mood for it'), not modern 'brave'. か … む: a rhetorical question, 'how could one be keen? (One couldn't.)'.

notes.quote: 心は縁にひかれて移るものなれば
notes.text: {縁|えん}: a Buddhist word for the conditions around you, everything that touches the mind from outside. The whole argument for leaving home rests on this sentence.

いとなむ: 'to work at, to be busy with'. Here: a monk who still has to see to food and shelter, as in the sentence before. Many modern editions read 世をいとはむ人 instead, 'someone who turns away from the world'. The translation follows the 1925 text.

{藜|あかざ}: goosefoot, a common weed that poor people ate. The 1925 edition quotes the Chinese poet Han Yu on goosefoot soup as the food of the poor. {紙|かみ}の{衾|ふすま}: a blanket made of paper, the bedding of poor monks. {一鉢|いつぱつ}: the one bowl a monk eats from.

notes.quote: 形に恥づる所もあれば
notes.text: {形|かたち}: his appearance, the shaved head and the robes. He has the look of a monk, and he would be ashamed to act against it.
まほし: 'would like'. こそ … けれ closes the sentence with the realis form.
{菩提|ぼだい}: awakening, enlightenment, the end of the Buddhist path. あるまじくや: 'surely there would be no difference?'
